title: Don't spend a later step's evidence early
statement: No step may use up what a later one teaches or tests.
example: One lesson's follow-up keys repeated the guide's line just before them at 1.00 overlap, and measured 0 after the rewrite.
detail: A comparison of one course's branched follow-up checks measured how much each key repeated the guide's line just before it: one lesson echoed its answer at 1.00 overlap and another at 0.80, against 0.50 in a third, and both measured 0 after the rewrite; before it, the right answer had been the sentence the guide just said, word for word (`grade3-reading/artifacts/compare-2026-09-23/index.html`). An external audit of four lessons found a vocabulary check whose key reused the teaching card's own example, an early check whose key was the exact line the next page's worked model then 'finds', and a search step whose right answer named two of the three lines the next step asks for (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-inceptbench-2026-09-30/REGISTER.md`). A curriculum audit found an early check that spent the worked model's clue before the model used it (`grade3-reading/artifacts/curriculum-adherence-2026-09-24/REPORT.md`), and a gap list found a goal line that supplied the inference before the model asked for it (`grade3-reading/artifacts/peter-pan-standing-2026-09-11/PP-STANDING.md`). It is the step-to-step form of nothing-gives-the-answer-first. A key that repeats the line just heard, or the example that taught it, tests only echo, and an earlier line that names a later step's evidence or inference leaves that step nothing to do.
